Potential limitations of the use of stent-based thrombectomy
techniques in ABAO include the need for bilateral vertebral artery
occlusion to achieve effective aspiration during the thrombectomy
process. This would require a bifemoral approach with the use of
two catheter-balloon systems, making the procedure more compli-
cated and time consuming. The largest guiding catheter would be
placed at the dominant VA to serve as the aspiration catheter with
the second balloon occluding the contralateral VA. Our case was
technically facilitated by the already occluded contralateral verte-
bral and a single system achieved the desired occlusion–suction
effect.
A second limitation of this technique in the posterior circulation
is the reduced caliber of the VA. Reduced arterial diameter pre-
cludes routine use of the large guiding catheters (8 Fr) that are reg-
ularly used for carotid stroke therapies. In our patient, we selected
a 6 Fr catheter with no balloon tip, which effectively occluded the
sole access VA and enabled effective aspiration.
The devastating effects of this posterior circulation stroke were
not relieved in this patient. However, we were able to obtain com-
plete revascularization using the stent–thrombectomy approach
within 37 minutes. With earlier detection of the basilar occlusion,
this approach could prove life saving in some patients.
In conclusion, we present the successful technical use of a
stent-based thrombectomy technique ABAO. This technique is
promising and will need further evaluation in posterior circula-
tion stroke.

Hyperexcitability restricted to the lower limb motor system in a patient with
stiff-leg syndrome
Tomonori Iwata a,/C160, Hiroshi Shigeto a,⇑,/C160, Katsuya Ogata b, Ko-ichi Hagiwara a, Yuji Kanamori a, Taira Uehara a,
Yasumasa Ohyagi a, Shozo Tobimatsu b, Jun-ichi Kira a
a Department of Neurology, Neurological Institute, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kyushu University, Higashi-ku, Maidashi 3-1-1, Fukuoka 81 2-8582, Japan

b Department of Clinical Neurophysiology, Neurological Institute, Graduate School of Medical Sciences, Kyushu University, Fukuoka, Japan

abstract
We report a 29-year-old man who presented with a 2-year history of progressive stiffness and painful
spasms limited to the bilateral lower limbs, exaggerated by auditory and tactile stimuli. His deep tendon
reﬂexes were slightly increased in both lower extremities. His plantar response was ﬂexor. His serum and
cerebrospinal ﬂuid were negative for anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies. Electromyography of
antagonist muscle pairs in his distal lower limbs revealed a failure of reciprocal inhibition. We used trans-
cranial magnetic stimulation with a paired-pulse paradigm, delivered to the cortical area of the upper and
lower limbs, and revealed signiﬁcantly enhanced facilitation only in the area of his lower limbs, but not
that representing his upper limbs. His symptoms were improved substantially by 20 mg/day of oral diaz-
epam. To our knowledge this is the ﬁrst report of a patient with hyperexcitability limited to the lower
limb motor system in a patient with stiff-leg syndrome.

1. Introduction
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) and stiff-leg syndrome (SLS) are
considered autoimmune disorders, and are characterized by pro-
gressive stiffness and spontaneous reﬂex-induced, or action-in-
duced, painful muscle spasms. The former affects the trunk and
proximal limbs, while the latter affects the distal lower limbs. 1–4
Electromyography (EMG) ﬁndings for these diseases typically in-
clude continuous motor unit activity without reciprocal inhibition,
suggesting impairment of inhibitory systems in the spinal cord.
5 In
SPS, hyperexcitability in the cortical motor areas representing the
hands, in addition to spinal cord hyperexcitability, has been

demonstrated using paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimula-
tion (TMS).6 However, the cortical motor area representing the legs
has not been investigated in patients with SPS or SLS. Therefore, we
studied the excitability of the leg area of the motor cortex in a pa-
tient with SLS using paired-pulse TMS.
2. Case report
A 29-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of progres-
sive stiffness and painful spasms of the bilateral distal lower limbs.
On admission, cranial nerves, trunk and motor functions of the
upper limbs were normal. Both legs had a dorsiﬂexion posture with
painful spasms, which were exaggerated by auditory and tactile
stimuli (Fig. 1). He could walk very slowly with severe stiffness
and abnormal posturing of bilateral legs because of severe stiff-
ness. Deep tendon reﬂexes were slightly increased in both lower
limbs. The plantar response was ﬂexor.
Complete blood counts and serum chemistry were normal.
Cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) examination was unremarkable except
for the presence of oligoclonal bands. Anti-glutamic acid decarbox-
ylase (GAD) antibodies were not detected in serum or CSF. Autoan-
tibodies, including anti-amphiphysin antibodies, were also not
detected. There were no remarkable ﬁndings on electroencephalo-
gram, electrocardiogram, chest roentgenogram, CT scans of the
chest and abdomen or MRI of the brain and spinal cord. A nerve
conduction study including F-waves in all four limbs, single-pulse
motor-evoked potentials and somatosensory-evoked potentials of
the upper and lower limbs all had normal latencies. Surface
electromyogram (EMG) recording of the tibialis anterior (TA) and
soleus muscles revealed co-contraction of these antagonistic
muscles (Fig. 2).
Paired-pulse TMS was performed as described previously.
7 Gen-
erally, the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitudes
of the target muscle are reduced when the interstimulus intervals
(ISI) between the conditioning and test stimuli are 2–3 ms (intra-
cortical inhibition [ICI]), 8 but increased with ISI of 5–20 ms (intra-
cortical facilitation [ICF]). 9 In our patient, the target muscles were
the right abductor pollicis brevis (APB) for the upper limbs and the
right TA for the lower limbs. These tests were performed in the sit-
ting position and EMG were monitored audiovisually to ensure the
relaxation of the target muscles. EMG signals were ampliﬁed with
a bandpass ﬁlter between 10 Hz and 2000 Hz (Neuropack 8, Nihon
Kohden, Tokyo, Japan) using a pair of surface electrodes, and stored
on a personal computer with a sampling rate of 10 kHz. TMS was
delivered through a 70-mm ﬁgure-eight shaped coil with the cen-
ter over the left-hand motor area for right APB stimulation, while a
90-mm round coil was placed at about 5 cm anterior to the Cz for
right TA stimulation. Coils were connected to two Magstim 200
stimulators via a Bistim module (Magstim Co., Whitland, Dyfed,
UK). The conditioning stimulus intensity was set at 90% of the
active motor threshold, which was deﬁned as the lowest stimulus
intensity at which 5 out of 10 consecutive stimuli evoked a 100- lV

motor evoked potential (MEP) in the mildly contracted target mus-
cle. The test stimulus intensity was set at 115% of the motor
threshold in the same way as in the relaxed muscle. The same coil
produced conditioning and test stimuli, which had the same cur-
rent direction. Paired stimuli were delivered with ISI of 1, 4, 6, 8,
10, and 20 ms in a pseudorandom order in blocks of 10 trials for
each condition. MEP of test stimuli were also recorded in the same
blocks of 20 trials. The results are expressed as the ratios of the
CMAP amplitudes elicited by a test stimulus with a conditioning
stimulus relative to those elicited by an unconditioned stimu-
lus.9,10 The patient was compared with four normal controls (mean
age ±standard deviation [SD], 30.5 ± 7.5 years; two males, two
females).
In our patient the ICF of the TA were enhanced compared with
those of the controls with ISI of 6, 8 and 10 ms. In particular, the ICF
recorded with ISI of 8 and 10 ms exceeded the mean values of the
controls by more than 2 SD (Fig. 3 upper). However, the ICF of the
APB were unchanged (Fig. 3 lower).
Diazepam (20 mg/day in divided doses) markedly improved the
stiffness and painful spasms of the lower limbs. EMG ﬁndings were
also improved by the treatment (Fig. 2). Compared with the pre-
treatment value, a mild reduction in the ICF in AT recorded with
ISI of 10 and 20 ms was found during the therapy period, in line
with the loss of co-contraction (Fig. 3).
3. Discussion
Pathophysiological mechanisms of SLS and SPS are still unclear.
Both syndromes may overlap and have dysfunction in inhibitory
gamma-amino butyric acid (GABA)-ergic pathways arising from
autoimmune process. In SLS, incidence of anti-GAD antibody is
low and good response to GABA-ergic drugs and immune therapy
are obtained compared to SPS. We diagnosed the patient with hav-
ing SLS based on the lack of anti-GAD antibody and favorable re-
sponse to diazepam in addition to differences in the affected
body parts.
In our patient, ICF was not enhanced in the hand area, although
an enhanced ICF was observed in the leg area. ICF in the leg area
recorded with ISI of 8 and 10 ms was regarded as abnormal
because it exceeded the control level by more than 2 SD.
Treatment with diazepam partly diminished the enhanced ICF
with ISI of 10 and 20 ms. Indeed, ICF may reﬂect the activity of
excitatory cortical interneurons under GABA-ergic inhibitory con-
trol.
9,11 ICF with an ISI of 25 ms is considered to be of cortical ori-
gin, while the origin of ICF with ISI in the range of 10–25 ms is
unclear.12 Our ﬁndings in the present patient suggest that the
abnormal ICF in a limited area of the cortex may be induced by
the inﬂuence of disinhibited spinal cord neurons. However, we
cannot completely exclude the possibility that hyperexcitability
in the motor cortex restricted to the leg area might cause the con-
tinuous contractions of the distal lower limbs. Further examina-
tions in additional cases are required to elucidate the role of
cortical excitability in patients with SPS and SLS.
